query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a moderate amount of a heavy 5d element—in this case Au—in a balanced, equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy will trigger local lattice distortions and partial, L10‐like chemical ordering that increases magnetocrystalline anisotropy and domain‐wall pinning, thereby significantly raising the coercivity relative to the pure fcc FeCoNi baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: A sputtered, nearly pure equiatomic FeCoNi high-entropy alloy thin film having an fcc structure, high saturation magnetization, and low coercivity.
generation.intervention: Replace one quarter of the magnetic sublattice by Au to form an equiatomic four‐component (Fe, Co, Ni, Au) alloy (i.e. ~25 at.% each) so that the overall configurational entropy remains above 1.0R.
generation.conditions: Prepare thin films by sputtering onto Si/SiO2 substrates and then apply rapid thermal annealing (RTA) under conditions similar to past studies (e.g., deposition at moderate substrate temperature and RTA lasting 15–30 s) to facilitate the onset of local chemical ordering while preserving the high-entropy state.
generation.structural_mediator: Local tetragonal lattice distortions and incipient L10-like chemical ordering induced by the size and spin–orbit characteristics of Au atoms.
generation.mechanism: Due to its large atomic radius and strong spin–orbit coupling, Au in moderate amounts will locally break the fcc symmetry of the FeCoNi matrix. This reduced local symmetry can enhance magnetocrystalline anisotropy and promote directional strain fields that serve as effective pinning sites for magnetic domain walls. Consequently, the coercivity is increased even while the overall high saturation magnetization is largely maintained.
generation.predicted_outcome: The resulting equiatomic FeCoNiAu alloy is predicted to exhibit a coercivity several times higher (for example, 3- to 10-fold increase) than the pure FeCoNi alloy, while retaining a magnetic moment comparable to that of the unmodified system.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited, pure equiatomic FeCoNi high-entropy alloy thin film with fcc symmetry, high saturation magnetization, and a low coercive field.
generation.boundary: This intervention applies specifically to high-entropy thin film systems processed under conditions (e.g., sputtering plus RTA) that enable retention of equiatomic composition and high configurational entropy. Behavior in bulk systems, other processing routes, or under significantly different thermal treatments may differ.
generation.uncertainty: The proposal builds on the observation that heavy-element (e.g., Pt) induced ordering via RTA can dramatically boost coercivity (as seen in PMC11426066::web::012 and PMC11426066::web::019), yet previous investigations using high fractions of Pt or Pd in FeCoNi derivatives resulted in soft magnets. The uncertainty lies in whether substituting Au—whose large atomic size and strong spin–orbit coupling may prompt local ordering without overly reducing configurational entropy—can strike the correct balance. This extension from Pt studies to a moderate Au intervention is novel and untested in this system.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of thin film samples: one set of pure equiatomic FeCoNi films and a second set of equiatomic FeCoNiAu films (with 25 at.% each element). Employ identical sputtering and RTA processing conditions. Characterize both sets by X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to detect any local lattice distortions or indications of L10-like ordering. Then, measure their magnetic properties—particularly coercivity and saturation magnetization—using vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM).
measurements: Evidence of local symmetry breaking or peak splitting in XRD
Microstructural details from TEM (such as local distortions or ordering)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the FeCoNiAu samples do not show a statistically significant (e.g., greater than 2×) increase in coercivity relative to the pure FeCoNi baseline, or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal any indications of the intended local ordering or lattice distortion, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Certain HEA compositions may exhibit long‐range chemical order through the emergence of multiple sublattices, analogous to high entropy ceramics,[  ] leading to so‐called “high entropy intermetallic” (HEI) compounds.[  ] Previously, transition metal alloys with high anisotropy, such as the L10 phases of FePt and FePd have been achieved by annealing of equiatomic solid solution pre‐cursors.[  ] In the case of metastable high anisotropy phases such as L10 FeNi, unconventional annealing techniques have been employed.[  ] In particular, rapid thermal annealing (RTA) of transition metal alloy films on Si/SiO2 is an effective means of inducing high anisotropy phase formation in solid solution precursors, in part due to the substrate‐induced strain.[  ] In this study, we experimentally demonstrate two thin film HEAs with large coercivity and magnetic anisotropy achieved by RTA. We show that RTA treatment of equiatomic FeCoNiMnCu thin films leads to ≈40‐fold increase in coercivity. By introduction of 50 at.% Pt, we realize an L10 HEI phase of (FeCoNiMnCu)Pt with perpendicular magnetic anisotropy resulting from a reduced lattice symmetry and strong spin‐orbit coupling. While the combination of saturation magnetization and coercivity for these RTA‐ treated FeCoNiMnCu films is impressive in comparison to previously reported bulk systems, the coercivity is still modest, due to the high symmetry of the cubic lattice which limits the intrinsic magnetocrystalline anisotropy. The facilitation of low‐symmetry chemical order and crystal structure combined with strong spin‐orbit coupling is in general necessary to realize strong magnetocrysalline anisotropy. To achieve these conditions in a high entropy system, we have added 50 at.% Pt to the FeCoNiMnCu alloy, employing the high entropy intermetallic design approach in search of highly anisotropic L10 ordering. Although the certainty of Pt sites reduces the configurational entropy compared to the equiatomic case, we demonstrate below that such optimized entropy can still stabilize a single high‐entropy L10 phase.

In summary, we have achieved high magnetic anisotropy in rare‐earth‐free high entropy metallic thin films by sputtering and RTA. Robust magnetic order of both fcc FeCoNiMnCu and L10 (FeCoNiMnCu)Pt films has been demonstrated. The FeCoNiMnCu films exhibit a large coercivity increase after RTA, resulting from microstructural changes and strain‐induced anisotropy enhancement which strengthens domain wall pinning. Addition of Pt reduces the symmetry of the cubic fcc lattice to an intermetallic tetragonal L10 phase of (FeCoNiMnCu)Pt. Although the Pt insertion lowers the configurational entropy compared to the equiatomic case, the entropy is still high enough to stabilize an L10 single phase. This intermetallic phase is confirmed to host high magnetocrystalline anisotropy, likely attributed to the lower symmetry of the L10 structure and the strong spin‐orbit coupling provided by the Pt insertion. These findings demonstrate the promise of high‐entropy intermetallic design as a key avenue to search for new high‐entropy magnets beyond the equiatomic composition.
